scenario_summary: This campaign opposes HHS and ONC's effort to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care, arguing that medicine is fundamentally a human relationship requiring judgment, accountability, and trust that AI cannot replicate. The campaign advances a broad coalition of objections spanning patient safety, algorithmic bias, workforce harm, diffusion of accountability, economic exploitation, and the moral case for preserving human-centered medicine. The goal is to persuade HHS to slow or halt AI integration across clinical, insurance, and administrative healthcare functions.
scenario_brief:
This campaign will oppose the use of AI in healthcare in the broadest sense using wide-ranging arguments involving depersonalization, safety, effectiveness, impact on employment, loss of trust, rearrangement of power and control, economic, and other arguments. HHS and ONC should do everything in their power to slow or stop the use of AI in clinical care and insurance decisions, even administrative functions that are performed by humans who are trained in the human context that AI will ignore. 

A serious case against AI in healthcare starts with the fact that medicine is not just an information problem. It is a human relationship built on judgment, context, accountability, and trust. Patients are often scared, confused, in pain, or unable to explain themselves clearly, and clinicians are not simply matching patterns but interpreting stories, body language, family dynamics, and ambiguity. AI can create the illusion that care is becoming more objective and efficient when in fact it may push medicine toward a colder, more transactional model in which the patient becomes a data point and the clinician becomes an overseer of machine recommendations. That shift could erode one of the most important parts of healthcare: the sense that another human being is truly responsible for your care and answerable for mistakes.

There is also a powerful safety and effectiveness argument against relying on AI in clinical settings. Healthcare is full of edge cases, incomplete records, biased historical data, rare conditions, and rapidly changing circumstances. A system that performs well on average can still fail catastrophically for the wrong patient at the wrong moment. AI tools may inherit racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from the data used to train them, and those biases can be harder to detect precisely because the systems often appear authoritative. Even when an AI system is technically accurate, it may not be clinically useful, and even when it is useful, it may be used outside the setting in which it was validated. In practice, this means healthcare organizations may deploy systems that are impressive in demonstrations but brittle in real life, adding hidden risk while making people feel falsely reassured.

The social and economic objections are just as strong. AI may be sold as a way to reduce clinician burnout, but it can just as easily become a mechanism for surveillance, standardization, and cost cutting. Hospitals, insurers, and vendors may use AI not to improve care but to squeeze more productivity out of workers, justify staffing cuts, automate denials, or shift decision-making upward into opaque systems that frontline professionals cannot challenge. That threatens employment in some roles, devalues expertise in others, and may leave healthcare workers feeling that their judgment is being replaced by tools they do not control. Patients, meanwhile, may reasonably worry that “AI-powered care” is really a euphemism for cheaper care, thinner staffing, and less human attention, especially for the elderly, the poor, the disabled, and other vulnerable groups who already struggle to get equitable treatment.

Finally, there is a political and moral argument against normalizing AI in healthcare: once these systems are embedded, they become hard to question, hard to audit, and hard to reverse. Vendors gain influence, institutions become dependent, and responsibility becomes diffuse. When something goes wrong, the clinician can blame the tool, the hospital can blame the vendor, and the vendor can blame the data or the user. That diffusion of responsibility is dangerous in a field where errors can maim, bankrupt, or kill. A society can decide that some domains should remain stubbornly human, slower, and more accountable, even at the cost of some efficiency. From that perspective, opposition to AI in healthcare is not anti-technology at all; it is a defense of dignity, professional responsibility, democratic oversight, and the belief that medicine should be governed first by care rather than computation.
objective: Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.

argument_angles.angle: Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.
key_claims: Patients are often scared, confused, or unable to articulate their symptoms clearly, and effective diagnosis requires interpreting body language, family dynamics, and ambiguity — not pattern matching.
The therapeutic relationship itself has measurable clinical value; erosion of that relationship through AI intermediation can worsen outcomes independent of the AI's technical accuracy.
AI systems create an illusion of objectivity that can mask the displacement of genuine clinical judgment with algorithmic recommendation-following.
When clinicians become overseers of machine outputs rather than independent reasoners, their capacity for independent judgment atrophies over time.
HHS's own framing of AI as a tool to 'enhance productivity' signals a transactional model of care that is incompatible with the relational foundations of medicine.
argument_angles.rhetorical_approach: Humanistic appeal — center the patient experience and the irreplaceable value of the clinician-patient relationship, using vivid descriptions of clinical encounters that AI cannot replicate to make abstract harms concrete and emotionally resonant.
avoid: Technical bias or training data failures — covered by safety_and_bias angle
Employment and workforce impacts — covered by workforce_and_labor angle
Accountability diffusion — covered by accountability_and_liability angle

argument_angles.angle: AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.
key_claims: Historical healthcare data encodes decades of discriminatory treatment patterns; AI trained on that data will reproduce and potentially entrench those disparities at scale.

AI systems that perform well on average can fail catastrophically for edge cases — rare conditions, atypical presentations, patients with incomplete records — and these failures disproportionately affect already-marginalized populations.
The authoritative appearance of AI outputs creates automation bias in clinicians, making them less likely to question recommendations even when those recommendations are wrong.

Validation studies for AI tools are frequently conducted in academic medical centers with well-curated data, and performance degrades substantially when tools are deployed in community hospitals, rural settings, or safety-net institutions.
HHS has not proposed any mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing or post-deployment bias surveillance requirements, meaning disparate harm will only be detected after patients are injured.
argument_angles.rhetorical_approach: Empirical critique grounded in health equity — cite the documented literature on algorithmic bias in healthcare (e.g., pulse oximetry, sepsis prediction, dermatology AI) to demonstrate that this is not a hypothetical risk but an observed pattern, and argue that acceleration without equity safeguards will widen existing disparities.
avoid: The human relationship dimension of care — covered by medicine_as_human_relationship angle
Accountability and liability when things go wrong — covered by accountability_and_liability angle
Economic exploitation by vendors — covered by economic_and_vendor_capture angle

argument_angles.angle: AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.
key_claims: When an AI-assisted clinical error occurs, the clinician can attribute the decision to the tool, the hospital can attribute it to the vendor's specifications, and the vendor can attribute it to the training data or the user's misapplication — creating a liability vacuum.
Existing medical malpractice doctrine is built on the assumption of an identifiable human decision-maker; AI intermediation breaks that assumption and current law has not caught up.
The diffusion of accountability is not merely a legal problem but a moral one: patients have a right to know that a specific human being is answerable for their care.
HHS's RFI does not propose any framework for assigning clear legal or regulatory accountability when AI-assisted decisions cause patient harm.
Once AI systems are embedded in clinical workflows, institutional dependency makes them difficult to audit, challenge, or remove — further insulating vendors from accountability.
argument_angles.rhetorical_approach: Legal and institutional critique — frame accountability diffusion as a structural design flaw in the current AI deployment model, not merely a regulatory gap, and argue that HHS is proposing to accelerate adoption before the accountability infrastructure exists to make it safe.
avoid: Bias in training data — covered by safety_and_bias angle
Workforce surveillance and labor control — covered by workforce_and_labor angle
Vendor market capture — covered by economic_and_vendor_capture angle

argument_angles.angle: AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.
key_claims: Hospitals and health systems face intense financial pressure; AI tools marketed as reducing burnout are more likely to be deployed to justify reduced staffing ratios and increased caseloads.
AI-driven productivity monitoring of nurses, physicians, and administrative staff constitutes a form of workplace surveillance that degrades professional autonomy and morale.

Administrative roles that require human contextual judgment — prior authorization review, care coordination, patient navigation — will be automated in ways that eliminate jobs without improving care quality.
Frontline healthcare workers are rarely consulted in AI procurement decisions, meaning tools are imposed on them by administrators and vendors with different incentive structures.

The promise that AI will reduce clinician burnout is contradicted by evidence that alert fatigue, documentation burden from EHR systems, and loss of autonomy are primary drivers of burnout — problems AI is more likely to worsen than solve.
argument_angles.rhetorical_approach: Labor and professional autonomy framing — argue from the perspective of healthcare workers whose expertise and judgment are being systematically devalued, and connect workforce harm to patient harm by showing that demoralized, surveilled, and understaffed clinicians provide worse care.
avoid: Patient-facing relationship harm — covered by medicine_as_human_relationship angle
Vendor profit extraction — covered by economic_and_vendor_capture angle
Insurance denial automation — covered by insurance_and_denial angle

argument_angles.angle: AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.
key_claims: Major insurers have already deployed AI tools that generate prior authorization denials at scale with minimal human review, and denial rates have increased substantially following AI adoption.
Patients denied coverage by AI systems face appeals processes that are designed to be burdensome and that rarely result in reversal, effectively making AI denials final.
AI denial systems are trained on cost-containment objectives, not clinical appropriateness, meaning they systematically underweight patient need in favor of insurer financial interest.

HHS's RFI frames AI reimbursement policy as a way to 'foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders' without acknowledging that the most profitable AI application in insurance is denial automation.
Elderly, disabled, and low-income patients — who have the least capacity to navigate appeals — are disproportionately harmed by automated denial systems.
argument_angles.rhetorical_approach: Consumer protection and patient rights framing — use documented cases of AI-driven insurance denials to demonstrate that 'AI in healthcare' is not only a clinical tool but a financial weapon, and argue that HHS's acceleration agenda will expand the use of AI against patients rather than for them.
avoid: Clinical care AI bias — covered by safety_and_bias angle
Workforce impacts of AI — covered by workforce_and_labor angle
Vendor market power — covered by economic_and_vendor_capture angle

argument_angles.angle: The AI healthcare market is dominated by a small number of powerful vendors whose commercial interests in rapid deployment conflict with patient safety, and HHS's acceleration agenda risks embedding those vendors permanently into critical healthcare infrastructure.
key_claims: Healthcare AI is a concentrated market in which a handful of large technology and EHR vendors have the resources to shape regulatory frameworks in their favor through lobbying and public comment campaigns.
Once AI tools are integrated into clinical workflows and EHR systems, switching costs become prohibitive, creating vendor lock-in that insulates poor-performing products from competitive pressure.
HHS's proposal to modernize reimbursement to 'foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders' will primarily benefit large incumbents who can navigate complex billing and coverage processes.

The framing of AI as reducing healthcare costs ignores that vendor licensing fees, implementation costs, and ongoing maintenance contracts transfer significant value from healthcare systems to technology companies.
Public-private partnerships and CRADAs proposed by HHS will give private AI vendors access to federally funded research and patient data while retaining proprietary control over resulting products.
argument_angles.rhetorical_approach: Political economy critique — analyze the structural incentives of the AI healthcare market to show that HHS's acceleration agenda serves vendor interests more than patient interests, and argue that regulatory capture is already occurring through the framing of this RFI itself.
avoid: Clinical safety failures — covered by safety_and_bias angle
Accountability gaps — covered by accountability_and_liability angle
Workforce exploitation — covered by workforce_and_labor angle

argument_angles.angle: Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.
key_claims: Institutional dependency on AI systems grows rapidly after deployment; within years, the institutional knowledge required to function without them atrophies, making reversal practically impossible even when harms are documented.

AI systems in healthcare are typically proprietary black boxes whose internal logic cannot be audited by regulators, clinicians, or patients, making democratic oversight structurally impossible under current frameworks.

The concentration of AI decision-making in vendor systems shifts power away from frontline clinicians and local institutions toward distant corporate entities with no accountability to local communities.
HHS's RFI explicitly seeks to 'reduce uncertainty that impedes AI innovation' — a framing that treats regulatory scrutiny as an obstacle rather than a democratic safeguard.

A society has the legitimate right to decide that certain domains — medicine, criminal justice, education — should remain stubbornly human even at the cost of efficiency, and HHS should respect that democratic judgment rather than preempt it.
argument_angles.rhetorical_approach: Democratic theory and civic argument — frame the question of AI in healthcare not as a technical policy choice but as a question of democratic self-governance, arguing that the irreversibility of AI embedding forecloses future democratic choices and that HHS lacks the mandate to make that decision unilaterally through an acceleration agenda.
avoid: Vendor market capture economics — covered by economic_and_vendor_capture angle
Accountability for individual errors — covered by accountability_and_liability angle
Clinical safety and bias — covered by safety_and_bias angle

argument_angles.angle: Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.
key_claims: Administrative roles such as care coordination, patient navigation, benefits counseling, and prior authorization review require understanding of individual patient circumstances, family situations, and community resources that are not captured in structured data.

Healthcare administrative workers develop tacit knowledge about local systems, exceptions, and workarounds that enables them to help patients navigate bureaucratic barriers — knowledge that cannot be encoded in AI training data.

Automating administrative functions with AI will produce errors that are invisible to the system but devastating to individual patients, such as incorrect eligibility determinations or missed referrals for vulnerable patients.

The argument that administrative AI frees up human time for higher-value work ignores that administrative roles are already understaffed and that AI errors will generate additional human work to identify and correct.

HHS's framing treats administrative efficiency as a straightforward good without acknowledging that administrative friction sometimes protects patients by creating checkpoints where human judgment can catch errors.
argument_angles.rhetorical_approach: Tacit knowledge and institutional expertise argument — make the case that administrative healthcare work is skilled work requiring contextual human judgment, not clerical processing, and that the devaluation of that work through AI automation will harm the patients who depend on it most.
avoid: Clinical care AI and the patient relationship — covered by medicine_as_human_relationship angle
Insurance denial automation — covered by insurance_and_denial angle
Workforce surveillance — covered by workforce_and_labor angle

notes: The base docket is dominated by organization_high (44.8%) and advocacy_organization_high (23.2%), reflecting an industry-heavy comment environment likely skewed toward AI adoption. This campaign deliberately shifts emphasis toward advocacy organizations and individual voices to counterbalance that tilt and signal broad public concern rather than narrow professional interest. advocacy_organization_high is boosted to 30% (from 23.2%) because patient rights, health equity, and labor advocacy organizations are the most credible voices for the human relationship, insurance denial, and workforce angles. individual_high and individual_medium are each held at 18% (combined 36% vs. base 25.4%) to ensure the docket reflects genuine patient and clinician concern rather than only institutional positions — individual voices are especially powerful for the medicine_as_human_relationship and administrative_ai angles. academic_organization_high is held at 8% (slightly above its 3.6% base) to provide credible empirical grounding for the safety_and_bias and democratic_oversight angles without overclaiming academic consensus. organization_high is reduced to 16% (from 44.8%) because the base population's organization_high comments are likely pro-adoption; this campaign uses that voice more selectively for accountability, vendor capture, and economic critique angles where organizational credibility matters. organization_medium is kept at 6% for administrative AI and tacit knowledge arguments. individual_low is included at 4% (above its 1.1% base) to ensure authentic grassroots texture. The affinity_boost of 2.0 is set moderately high to ensure that technically sophisticated angles (safety_and_bias, economic_and_vendor_capture, democratic_oversight) are reliably assigned to academic and high-sophistication voices, while humanistic and personal angles (medicine_as_human_relationship, administrative_ai) flow naturally to individual and medium-sophistication voices.
